name: Ezekiel
v: When you parcel out the land as inheritance, set aside a sacred portion for the LORD — a holy district carved from the land itself: twenty-five thousand cubits long, twenty thousand wide. The whole stretch is holy ground.
Within it, mark off a perfect square for the sanctuary — five hundred by five hundred — ringed by fifty cubits of open space on every side.
From that holy district measure out a strip twenty-five thousand by ten thousand. The sanctuary itself stands there — the holy of holies.

This is the consecrated portion of the land, reserved for the priests who serve in the sanctuary, the ones who draw near to minister to the LORD. Here they will have houses. Here the sanctuary will stand.
Another strip, twenty-five thousand by ten thousand, belongs to the Levites who serve at the temple — towns of their own to live in.
Alongside the sacred portion, set aside the city's land: five thousand wide, twenty-five thousand long. This belongs to all Israel.

The prince gets the territory flanking both sides of the holy portion and the city's land — west to the Mediterranean, east to the eastern border — matching the length of one of the tribal allotments running from western sea to eastern frontier.
This land is his stake in Israel. And from now on my princes will stop crushing my people. They will leave the land to the house of Israel, tribe by tribe.

This is what the Lord GOD says: Enough, princes of Israel. End the violence. End the plunder. Do justice. Do righteousness. Stop evicting my people from their land. This is the declaration of the Lord GOD.
Use honest scales. Honest measures. Honest weights.
The ephah and the bath must be the same volume — both a tenth of a homer. The homer is the standard.
Twenty gerahs make a shekel. Sixty shekels make a mina.
Here is the offering you bring: a sixth of an ephah from every homer of wheat, the same from every homer of barley.
For oil — measured by the bath — give a tenth of a bath from every kor (the kor being ten baths, or one homer, since ten baths equal a homer).

And from the flock: one sheep out of every two hundred from the well-watered pastures of Israel. These are for grain offerings, burnt offerings, peace offerings — to make atonement for the people. This is the declaration of the Lord GOD.
Every citizen of the land must bring this offering to the prince of Israel.

And the prince — he carries the burden of the burnt offerings, the grain offerings, the drink offerings at the festivals, the new moons, the Sabbaths — every appointed gathering of the house of Israel. He provides the sin offering, the grain offering, the burnt offering, the peace offerings, to make atonement for the house of Israel.
This is what the Lord GOD says: On the first day of the first month, take a bull from the herd — flawless — and purify the sanctuary.
The priest takes some of the blood of the sin offering and smears it on the doorposts of the temple, on the four corners of the altar's ledge, on the doorposts of the gate to the inner court.
Do the same on the seventh day of the month for anyone who has sinned by mistake or ignorance. That is how you make atonement for the house.
On the fourteenth day of the first month — the Passover. A seven-day feast. You eat unleavened bread.
On that day the prince offers a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people of the land.
Through the seven days of the feast he provides burnt offerings to the LORD: seven bulls and seven rams, all flawless, day after day for seven days — and daily a male goat as a sin offering.
He provides a grain offering: an ephah for each bull, an ephah for each ram, with a hin of oil per ephah.
In the seventh month, on the fifteenth day, at the feast — same again. For seven days he provides the same sin offerings, burnt offerings, grain offerings, and oil.

com.d:
# Ezekiel 45: The Restoration of Holy Order

God's vision for restoration in Ezekiel 45 reveals something fundamental about His heart: a renewed people requires renewed spaces, renewed worship, and renewed justice. After judgment comes the promise of precise, intentional rebuilding—not haphazardly, but with the care of an architect who knows what His dwelling place should be.

This chapter prescribes the division of the land among priests, Levites, the city, and the prince, followed by detailed instructions for offerings and feasts. At first glance, it seems remote from contemporary life—we don't divide land by tribal inheritance or offer bulls at altars. Yet the underlying principle pulses with relevance. God cares about *how* we organize our corporate life together. He's not indifferent to justice in business dealings, proper worship, or how leadership functions in His community. The specificity itself matters; it demonstrates that holiness isn't vague or improvised but thoughtfully stewarded.

Notice the concern for honest weights and measures. God emphasizes that "You shall have just balances, a just ephah, and a just bath" (45:10). In our world of hidden algorithms, inflated claims, and financial deception, this ancient concern speaks loudly. God wants His people marked by integrity in the everyday transactions that bind community together. When we cheat in business, shade the truth in negotiations, or exploit systems for personal gain, we're not merely breaking a rule—we're rejecting God's vision for how His restored people should conduct themselves.

The passage culminates in the reinstitution of feasts and festivals, rhythmic gatherings where people remember God's faithfulness and realign themselves with His purposes. We might ask ourselves: in our busy, individualistic age, do we build enough sacred space for corporate worship and remembrance?

What specific area of your life might God be inviting you to bring into greater alignment with His vision of justice and holiness?
com.s:
Ezekiel 45 constitutes a crucial segment within the prophet's extended temple vision (chapters 40–48), presenting regulations for sacred space allocation and cultic practice in the idealized restoration community. Composed during the Babylonian exile, likely around 573 BCE based on the chronological marker in 40:1, this material reflects Ezekiel's priestly concerns and his vision for a purified Israel that would prevent the abominations that led to Jerusalem's destruction. The chapter divides into two primary sections: the apportionment of sacred land (vv. 1–8) and regulations governing offerings and festivals (vv. 9–25).

The opening verses introduce the concept of a *terumah* (תְּרוּמָה), a "contribution" or "heave offering" of land measuring 25,000 by 20,000 cubits, set apart as holy ground. This sacred district would contain the sanctuary, priestly residences, and Levitical territory, establishing concentric zones of holiness radiating outward from the temple. The term *qodesh* (קֹדֶשׁ), appearing repeatedly throughout the passage, emphasizes the fundamental distinction between sacred and profane that structures Ezekiel's entire visionary program.

Particularly significant is the attention given to the *nasi* (נָשִׂיא), rendered "prince" rather than "king," who receives designated territory flanking the sacred district. This terminology deliberately distances the future ruler from monarchical associations, perhaps reflecting Ezekiel's critique of pre-exilic royal abuses documented in verse 9's admonition against violence and oppression. The prince's responsibilities include providing offerings for atonement, suggesting a role subordinate to priestly authority rather than competing with it.

The chapter's latter portion establishes standardized weights and measures—the ephah, bath, and shekel—addressing economic justice alongside cultic regulation. The Passover and Festival of Booths receive detailed treatment, though scholars note the absence of Pentecost, prompting debate regarding textual completeness or deliberate theological selection. The prescribed sin offerings and burnt offerings demonstrate Ezekiel's systematic approach to atonement, with blood manipulation rituals cleansing the sanctuary on the first and seventh days of the first month. This material exhibits both continuity with Pentateuchal legislation and distinctive Ezekielian innovations, representing the prophet's comprehensive vision for reconstituting Israelite worship in conditions of purity and justice.
com.p:
Ezekiel chapter forty-five emerges from the prophet's exile in Babylon, written approximately 573 years before the incarnation of Christ, during the darkest period of Israel's national existence. The temple lay in ruins, the Davidic throne stood vacant, and the people languished in captivity. Yet here, in stunning prophetic vision, Ezekiel receives detailed instructions for a restored land, a holy district, and righteous governance—a vision whose ultimate fulfillment stretches from the post-exilic return through the church age and into the eternal kingdom yet to come.

Within the grand redemptive arc, this passage stands at the threshold between exile and restoration, pointing backward to the Mosaic covenant's sacrificial system while simultaneously gesturing forward to realities that transcend anything Israel experienced after returning from Babylon. The holy district described here, with its careful divisions for the sanctuary, priests, Levites, and city, establishes a sacred geography centered entirely on the presence of God. This territorial holiness echoes Eden's original design and anticipates the New Jerusalem where God dwells permanently among His people.

The prince figure in this chapter presents a fascinating typological puzzle. Unlike the corrupt kings who led Israel into exile, this ruler provides sacrifices for the people, ensures just weights and measures, and serves rather than exploits. He is both Davidic and yet distinct from the Messiah who needs no sin offering for himself. The prince shadows Christ's kingly office while the regulations surrounding him expose by contrast the perfect righteousness of the true King who offered not bulls and goats but Himself as the once-for-all sacrifice.

The appointed feasts—Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles—receive prominent attention, binding this future vision to Israel's foundational salvation narratives. The Passover lamb slain for the household points eternally to Christ our Passover, sacrificed for us. These observances in Ezekiel's temple vision remind the church that all Old Testament worship found its substance in the Lamb who takes away the sin of the world.

The remarkable emphasis on just measurements and honest commerce reveals that true restoration involves ethical transformation, not merely ritual precision. The God who weighs hearts demands integrity in weights and measures.

For the church dwelling between Christ's two advents, Ezekiel forty-five declares that God's ultimate intention remains unchanged: a people dwelling in holiness around His presence, governed by justice, marked by true worship, awaiting the day when shadow yields completely to substance.
